To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the recovery of biota in acid sensitive lakes in Canada is expected to be greatest for lakes with the highest pH and lowest DOC content, and for the largest lakes.

(1) The greatest recovery of biota in aquatic systems in southeastern Canada is likely to occur during the final phase (between 1994 and the end of the century) of sulphate deposition reductions, with a greater recovery predicted for Ontario regions than southcentral Québec and Kejimujik; (2) The greatest recovery is predicted for zooplanktons, followed by benthic macroinvertebrates and fish.

(1) acidic deposition has had a major negative effect on aquatic ecosystems, particularly in regions of high deposition, (2) the most sensitive species and groups are the most vulnerable and will be the slowest to recover, (3) the most important indicator species are different in each region, and (4) there is still potential for recovery in all regions, but this recovery potential is greatest in the Ontario regions, and least in southcentral Québec.
In summary, our research is concerned with
assessing potential for recovery of biodiversity and indicator species due to changes in acidic deposition and lake pH in five areas of southeastern Canada.
predicting the potential recovery of biotic richness and indicator species in response to changes in acid deposition and lake pH.

developing a better understanding of how changes in acidic deposition and lake pH affect biotic communities in aquatic ecosystems, and how this information can be used to predict the recovery of biota in response to emission reductions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the greatest potential for biotic recovery in aquatic ecosystems in southeastern Canada is likely to occur after a further 20–25 years of sulphate emission reductions.
, for the five regions examined here, the most important factors in determining recovery potential are pH, DOC and size of the lake.
, although there will be a recovery of some species, it will be incomplete.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most sensitive indicator species in our analyses would not be able to recover to pre-1983 levels even with the full implementation of the AQA.
the recovery of biota in lakes with pH 4.0–6.0, as a result of sulphate deposition reductions, will be slow and will not be complete for decades, even with aggressive emission reduction scenarios.
the most sensitive species and communities are likely to recover to a lesser degree than the most tolerant species and communities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of acidification are not easily reversed and that recovery of aquatic biota will be a slow and protracted process.
there is no simple, single indicator species or taxonomic group that can be used to describe biotic recovery in response to emission reductions.

there is a great need for more data on the distribution and abundance of aquatic organisms in lakes and streams in order to better understand and predict recovery of aquatic biota in response to changes in acidic deposition and pH.
